To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Public bicycle and car share schemes have proliferated across the globe in recent years.
public bicycle and car share schemes are not currently socially inclusive in Glasgow, UK.

Public bicycle and car share schemes are increasingly part of urban transport landscapes, but there is a need for more research on their potential to promote social inclusion, and on the evaluation of schemes to measure their success or failure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the potential for shared mobility schemes to contribute to the development of a more socially inclusive transport system.
the question of whether or not shared transport schemes are inclusive and, if not, how they can be designed and managed in ways that make them more inclusive.
the question of whether shared transport schemes can be considered to be socially inclusive.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
shared schemes are not socially inclusive.
there is little evidence of social inclusion within the schemes.
there is no evidence to suggest that shared transport schemes are more socially inclusive than other modes of transport.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the bicycle and car share systems in Glasgow are neither socially equitable nor geographically accessible.
shared transport schemes are not yet inclusive modes of transport.
the spatial distribution of bike and car share schemes in Glasgow is inequitable and that this is not a problem of the location of the schemes but of the location of those who are able to use them.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the evaluation of such schemes needs to go beyond the simple counting of numbers of users and consider how they are distributed across the population, in particular in relation to their socio-economic status and the accessibility of the places where they live and work.
shared schemes are unlikely to be socially inclusive unless they are designed to be so and that this needs to be taken into account at the planning stage.

, while there are some benefits to be gained from shared transport, there is a need for more nuanced analysis of their impact and a need for more careful planning to ensure that they are socially inclusive.
